demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Rajan, at eighty years old, carried the weight of a lifetime's service in the Coast Guard, but more profoundly, the indelible scar of an accident decades ago that had shattered his sense of self. He had been on patrol near a remote marine sanctuary, the air thick with the scent of pine and salt, when a momentary lapse in judgment led to a collision with a small recreational craft. The image of the young boater, severely injured, was etched into his mind, along with the piercing wail of the rescue sirens that followed.

In the immediate aftermath, his memories of the event became fragmented pieces; he found it incredibly hard to deliberately recall the full sequence, as if parts of his mind had simply gone dark. Instead, the trauma would return in full sensory reliving, the sudden flash of sunlight on water, the distinct metallic tang of blood, the desperate cries-each fragment feeling completely real across all his senses at once, making him feel as if he was back there in that moment of horror. These disconnected, vivid memories became potent triggers, causing a surge of panic and a profound sense of threat. The world began to feel inherently dangerous, and he developed a pervasive hypervigilance, constantly on guard, convinced that something terrible was always about to happen. It was this very sense of impending threat that seemed to pull the fragmented memories to the surface, especially when his guard was down, forcing him to relive them as if to prepare for what might come next. This constant feeling of being threatened made him acutely sensitive to any reminders of the accident. Being in nature, especially near the coast or any body of water, became a powerful trigger, instantly flooding him with dread and making him feel threatened. Even the distant wail of a siren, a sound he once associated with duty, now instantly triggered a cascade of fear and brought back those fragmented, relived memories.

Rajan had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, a deep-seated defect that led to the accident. This character blame, this conviction that the event happened because of the sort of person he was, made him feel utterly exposed, and each encountered trigger only reinforced this painful appraisal. His belief that he was inherently flawed meant that seemingly innocuous details of his environment, like the scent of pine or the sight of distant water, became sharp reminders of his perceived failure, snagging his attention as potential signals of his own inherent danger. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, he desperately tried to push the thoughts out of his mind, employing thought suppression, and would force himself to think only positive thoughts, hoping to magically undo the past or at least numb the pain. His deep conviction that there was something defective about him fueled these desperate attempts to suppress thoughts and magically reframe reality, believing he couldn't handle the truth. The sheer horror of the full sensory reliving of his fragmented memories, too, made him double down on pushing them away and trying to distract himself with forced positive thoughts.

His constant feeling of being threatened made him hyper-attuned, turning mundane sounds or sights into triggers, and when he encountered a trigger, his sense of threat skyrocketed, confirming his belief that danger was everywhere. This pervasive threat drove him further into maladaptive strategies. He'd avoid unfamiliar places, feeling unable to assess the danger, and always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt, believing these actions would protect him. Paradoxically, these strategies, by limiting his engagement with the world, reinforced his belief that the world was indeed a dangerous place, thus maintaining his sense of threat. His attempts at thought suppression and magical thinking, by preventing him from processing the trauma, made the triggers even more potent and overwhelming when they inevitably broke through. This constant struggle, where his efforts to control his mind repeatedly failed, only solidified his conviction that something was inherently wrong with him, a weakness that made him incapable of facing his past. This inability to process and integrate his memories meant that sometimes, a specific fragment of memory would itself act as a new trigger, setting off a chain reaction. The relived memories themselves were terrifying, making him feel directly threatened by the past, and his constant hypervigilance and sense of impending doom only confirmed his deepest fear that he was inherently flawed and unworthy of safety. He had even developed a quiet disregard for his own well-being, taking too many risks in other areas of his life, as if his own safety no longer mattered because he was already defective.

In recent years, since his wife passed, Rajan's world had shrunk considerably. He refused to talk about the future, finding any discussion of plans or possibilities to be a potent trigger, filling him with an unshakeable dread that he would only cause further harm. His maladaptive strategies, while offering fleeting moments of relief, inadvertently contributed to his isolation and prevented any genuine processing of his past, sometimes even making it harder to deliberately recall the event, though the fragmented relivings persisted. He occasionally found that forcing positive thoughts offered a momentary reprieve from his crushing self-blame, but it never lasted. Now, after decades of living in the shadow of that day, the tightening grip of his past had become unbearable. A recent conversation with his nephew about moving closer to family, touching upon his future, had brought on a panic attack so severe it spurred him to seek help. He was tired of the constant vigilance, tired of the relentless fear, and hoped, against his deepest conviction, that there might still be something worth saving within him.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly state that Rajan's negative appraisals influence or lead to the presence or potency of his triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not explicitly state that Rajan's sense of threat directly influences or leads to the nature or frequency of his traumatic memories.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
